blocks.content: So far every type you have built could have any number of instances. But some concepts genuinely only ever have a small, fixed, known set of values, a traffic light is only ever red, yellow, or green, never anything else. An enum is exactly the tool for modeling that.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

An enum (short for enumeration) is a special type representing a fixed set of named constants. Unlike a regular class, you cannot create new instances of an enum beyond the ones it declares, RED, YELLOW, and GREEN are the only three TrafficLight values that will ever exist.

Without enums, developers used to represent fixed option sets with raw integers (0 for RED, 1 for YELLOW) or raw strings ("RED", "red", "Red"). Both approaches let completely invalid values slip through with zero compiler protection, an int meant to hold a traffic light state could just as easily hold 99, or a typo’d string could silently fail to match anything.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884685016-27964892.png
blocks.alt: The days of the week as a fixed, closed set of exactly seven named values

blocks.content: The days of the week are a perfect real-world enum: there are exactly seven of them, Monday through Sunday, and nothing else could ever be a valid "day of the week." You would never accept "Blursday" as a day, the set is completely closed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884686756-907029236.png
blocks.alt: A traffic light as a fixed set of exactly three named states

blocks.content: A traffic light is exactly the same idea: it is always red, yellow, or green, never a fourth color, never "sort of red." That fixed, closed set of options is precisely what an enum expresses in code.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884688242-12671700.png
blocks.alt: Raw int constants allowing any invalid value, replaced by an enum that only allows the real options

blocks.content: Enums solve the problem of representing a fixed set of options safely. Raw int or String constants give the compiler no way to reject an invalid value, a TrafficLight enum, by contrast, makes it impossible to even construct anything other than RED, YELLOW, or GREEN.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: An enum is a special data type that defines a fixed, named set of constants, and cannot be instantiated with any value outside that declared set. In simple terms: a closed list of named options the compiler actively enforces.
4. Key Terminology

["Enum constant: one of the fixed, named values an enum declares, like RED or GREEN.","Ordinal: the position of a constant in its declared order, starting at zero.","values(): a built-in method returning every constant of an enum, in declaration order.","valueOf(String): a built-in method that converts a matching string into its enum constant, or throws if there is no match.","Enum with fields and methods: in Java, an enum can carry its own fields and methods, exactly like a real class, since it effectively is one."]
items: Enum constant: one of the fixed, named values an enum declares, like RED or GREEN.
Ordinal: the position of a constant in its declared order, starting at zero.
values(): a built-in method returning every constant of an enum, in declaration order.
valueOf(String): a built-in method that converts a matching string into its enum constant, or throws if there is no match.
Enum with fields and methods: in Java, an enum can carry its own fields and methods, exactly like a real class, since it effectively is one.

items: RED(30), YELLOW(5), GREEN(25); declares exactly three constants, each passing its own value to the enum’s constructor.
TrafficLight(int durationSeconds) is the enum’s constructor, it runs exactly once per constant, when the enum type is first loaded.
next() is a regular method living on the enum, just like a method on any class, here it defines the RED to GREEN to YELLOW to RED cycle.
TrafficLight.values() returns an array of all three constants in the order they were declared, useful for looping over every possible value.

9. Behind the Scenes (Enums Are Real Classes)
blocks.text: 9. Behind the Scenes (Enums Are Real Classes)

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884692971-418325548.png
blocks.alt: An enum declaration compiling into a real class with exactly one instance per constant

blocks.content: In Java, an enum is not a special language trick, the compiler actually turns it into a full class, secretly extending java.lang.Enum. Each declared constant (RED, YELLOW, GREEN) becomes exactly one singleton instance of that class, created once, when the enum is first loaded, and reused forever after, this is why you can safely compare enum values with == instead of .equals().

11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["The compiler rejects any value outside the declared set, unlike raw ints or strings.","Adding a brand new constant later can require updating every switch statement that handles the enum exhaustively."],["Enum constants can safely be compared with ==, since each is a genuine singleton.","C++ enums are far more limited than Java’s, they cannot directly carry fields or methods the same way."],["In Java, an enum can carry its own fields and methods, making it a genuinely rich type, not just a label.","Enums are best for values truly fixed at compile time, they are the wrong tool for options that can change at runtime."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Using raw int or String constants for a fixed option set instead of an enum, losing all compiler-enforced safety.","Comparing enum values with .equals() out of habit, when == is both safe and idiomatic for enums.","Forgetting to update every switch statement over an enum when a new constant is added later.","Assuming C++ enums can carry fields and methods the same rich way Java enums can, they generally cannot without extra wrapper code."]
items: Using raw int or String constants for a fixed option set instead of an enum, losing all compiler-enforced safety.
Comparing enum values with .equals() out of habit, when == is both safe and idiomatic for enums.
Forgetting to update every switch statement over an enum when a new constant is added later.
Assuming C++ enums can carry fields and methods the same rich way Java enums can, they generally cannot without extra wrapper code.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Reach for an enum any time a value is genuinely one of a small, fixed, known set of options.","Put behavior that varies per constant directly on the enum itself (like next() above) instead of scattering switch statements everywhere.","Use values() to iterate safely over every possible constant instead of hardcoding a list elsewhere.","Let compile-time exhaustiveness checks (where the language supports them) help catch missing cases when a new constant is added."]
items: Reach for an enum any time a value is genuinely one of a small, fixed, known set of options.
Put behavior that varies per constant directly on the enum itself (like next() above) instead of scattering switch statements everywhere.
Use values() to iterate safely over every possible constant instead of hardcoding a list elsewhere.
Let compile-time exhaustiveness checks (where the language supports them) help catch missing cases when a new constant is added.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked "why prefer an enum over int constants," the fastest correct answer is: an enum gives the compiler a fixed, closed set of valid values to enforce, an int constant is just a number, nothing stops an invalid or out-of-range value from being passed in its place.
